lessons.title: Energy Sources and Consumption
lessons.body:
Smelting is energy-intensive. In Africa, most smelters use electricity, coal, coke, or diesel. For example, a typical electric arc furnace consumes 400â600 kWh per tonne of steel. A cupola furnace uses about 100â150 kg of coke per tonne of iron. Knowing your energy mix is the first step to managing costs and emissions.

Start by measuring how much energy you use. Install electricity meters on main feeders and sub-meters on large motors. For fuel, track kilograms of coke or litres of diesel per tonne of product. A simple spreadsheet with daily readings works. In South Africa, Eskom charges higher rates during peak hours (7â10 am and 6â8 pm). Shifting melting to off-peak can cut electricity bills by 20â30%.

Common energy sources in African smelting: grid electricity (often coal-heavy), diesel generators (for backup or remote sites), coal/coke (for reduction and heat), and increasingly solar PV or biomass briquettes. For example, a foundry in Kenya might use charcoal made from agricultural waste to fire a crucible furnace. In Nigeria, natural gas is used in some reheat furnaces.

To reduce consumption, check for leaks in compressed air lines, keep furnace doors closed, and preheat scrap using waste heat. A 10% reduction in energy use can increase profit margins significantly. Train operators to record energy data and report anomalies. Simple actions like fixing steam leaks or insulating pipes can save thousands of dollars per year.

Finally, consider renewable options. A 10 kW solar system can power lighting and small motors, reducing diesel use. But be realistic: smelting needs high power, so solar alone is rarely enough. Hybrid systems with batteries and generators are more practical. Start with an energy audit â many African utilities offer free or subsidised audits for industries.

lessons.title: Heat Recovery Systems
lessons.body:
In smelting, a lot of heat goes up the stack or into cooling water. Heat recovery captures that waste heat and uses it elsewhere, cutting fuel bills. For example, a furnace off-gas can be 400â800Â°C. Instead of venting it, you can pass it through a heat exchanger to preheat combustion air or scrap.

Common systems: recuperators (metal or ceramic) for preheating air; waste heat boilers to make steam for space heating or process; and thermal oil systems for lower temperatures. A simple shell-and-tube heat exchanger can recover 30â50% of flue gas heat. In a typical African foundry, preheating combustion air to 300Â°C can save 15â20% of fuel.

Installation steps: first, measure off-gas temperature and flow rate. Use a thermocouple and pitot tube. Then select a heat exchanger sized for your flow. For dusty gases, use a cyclone pre-cleaner to avoid fouling. Insulate all hot pipes with rock wool or ceramic fibre. Payback is often 1â3 years.

Case example: A steel rolling mill in Egypt installed a recuperator on a reheat furnace. They preheated air to 450Â°C, saving 25% of natural gas. In South Africa, a ferrochrome smelter used waste heat to dry ore, reducing moisture and saving coke. Even small operations can recover heat from cooling water using a plate heat exchanger to warm wash water or offices.

Maintenance is key: clean heat exchanger surfaces regularly (soot and dust reduce efficiency). Monitor pressure drop â a rise means blockage. Train operators to log temperatures and pressures daily. If you cannot afford a full system, start with simple insulation and sealing leaks. Every degree of heat recovered is money saved. Remember, heat recovery also reduces emissions because less fuel is burned.

lessons.title: Off-gas Treatment and Dust Collection
lessons.body:
Smelting produces off-gas laden with dust, metals, and toxic gases like sulphur dioxide (SO2) and carbon monoxide (CO). In Africa, many small smelters release these untreated, harming workers and nearby communities. Proper treatment is required by law in most countries and protects health.

First, capture the gas at the source. Use hoods over furnace openings and sealed charging systems. Then cool the gas if needed â a water quench or dilution air. Next, remove dust using cyclones (for coarse particles), baghouse filters (for fine dust), or electrostatic precipitators (for large volumes). A baghouse with polyester bags can capture 99% of dust, but must be kept below 130Â°C. For high temperatures, use ceramic or PTFE bags.

For SO2, scrub with lime or caustic soda in a packed tower. A simple venturi scrubber can remove both dust and SO2. In Zambia, copper smelters use acid plants to convert SO2 into sulphuric acid, which is sold. Small operations can use dry sorbent injection with hydrated lime.

Dust collected is often hazardous (contains lead, cadmium, zinc). Store in sealed bags or drums, label clearly, and dispose at licensed facilities. Never dump on open ground. In many African countries, waste manifest systems track hazardous waste.

Monitoring: install a continuous opacity monitor or use a portable dust monitor. Check for visible emissions â if you see smoke, something is wrong. Train workers to wear N95 masks and avoid direct contact. Regular maintenance of bags, valves, and fans is essential. A well-designed system costs money but prevents fines, lawsuits, and health problems. Start with a cyclone and baghouse â they are affordable and effective.

lessons.title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions
lessons.body:
Smelting emits greenhouse gases (GHGs) mainly carbon dioxide (CO2) from fuel combustion and chemical reactions. For example, producing one tonne of steel emits about 1.8 tonnes of CO2. Aluminium smelting emits about 1.5 tonnes CO2 per tonne if using coal power. In Africa, where many grids are coal-heavy, emissions are high.

Calculate your emissions: for electricity, multiply kWh by grid emission factor (e.g., South Africa ~0.95 kg CO2/kWh, Kenya ~0.1 kg CO2/kWh). For diesel, use 2.68 kg CO2 per litre. For coke, 3.1 kg CO2 per kg. Add process emissions from limestone or carbon electrodes. A simple spreadsheet can track monthly totals.

Reduce emissions by improving energy efficiency, switching to cleaner fuels (natural gas instead of coal, or biomass), and using renewable electricity. For example, a foundry in Morocco installed solar panels to power cranes and lighting, cutting 20% of CO2. Another in Ghana replaced charcoal with agricultural waste briquettes, reducing net CO2 because the waste would otherwise decompose.

Carbon credits: some African projects can earn credits under the Gold Standard or Verra. For example, a project that captures methane from landfill to fuel a furnace can sell credits. But the process is complex; start with measuring and reporting.

Regulations: many African countries now require GHG reporting. South Africa has a carbon tax (R120 per tonne CO2e as of 2024). Companies must report to the Department of Environment. Even if not required, measuring emissions helps identify savings. Set a target: reduce CO2 by 10% in two years. Train staff on energy and emissions. Small changes add up â a 5% reduction in CO2 often means 5% lower energy costs.

lessons.title: Energy Efficiency Best Practices
lessons.body:
Energy efficiency is the cheapest way to cut costs and emissions. Start with a walk-through audit: check for leaks, insulation gaps, and idle equipment. Use a thermal camera (or infrared thermometer) to find hot spots. In a typical African smelter, 10â20% of energy is wasted.

Top practices: 1) Preheat scrap or charge using waste heat. 2) Maintain burners â clean nozzles, set air-fuel ratios with a flue gas analyser (target 2â3% oxygen). 3) Seal furnace doors and use proper gaskets. 4) Insulate pipes, ladles, and furnaces with ceramic fibre or rock wool. 5) Replace oversized motors with high-efficiency ones (IE3 or IE4). 6) Use variable frequency drives (VFDs) on fans and pumps â can save 30â50%. 7) Schedule melting during off-peak hours. 8) Recover heat from cooling water for space heating.

Case: A steel mill in Tanzania reduced electricity by 15% by installing VFDs on dust collector fans and fixing compressed air leaks. Payback was 8 months. A copper smelter in DRC saved 20% of diesel by preheating combustion air with a recuperator.

Train operators: they control the process. Give them targets and feedback. Post energy use per tonne daily. Use simple tools: clamp meters, infrared thermometers, and flue gas analysers. Keep a log of energy use and production. Benchmark against similar plants â if you use 600 kWh/t and a competitor uses 500, find out why.

Maintenance is efficiency: dirty filters, worn belts, and misaligned pumps waste energy. Implement a weekly checklist. Also, consider cogeneration if you have waste heat â a steam turbine can generate electricity. But start with no-cost and low-cost measures first. Many utilities offer rebates for efficient equipment. In South Africa, Eskomâs IDM programme funds efficiency projects. In Kenya, KPLC has similar schemes. Ask your utility.

lessons.title: Regulatory Compliance and Reporting
lessons.body:
African countries have different environmental and energy regulations. You must know your national laws. In South Africa, the National Environmental Management: Air Quality Act (NEMAQA) requires an Atmospheric Emission Licence (AEL) for smelters. You must monitor and report emissions annually. The Carbon Tax Act requires reporting if you emit over 0.1 megatonnes CO2e.

In Nigeria, NESREA enforces the National Environmental (Air Quality) Regulations. Smelters need permits and must submit quarterly emission reports. In Kenya, NEMA requires an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and annual environmental audits. Ghanaâs EPA has similar rules. Penalties for non-compliance include fines, shutdown, and imprisonment.

Key steps: 1) Identify your regulator (environment agency, energy ministry). 2) Obtain necessary permits before construction. 3) Install monitoring equipment â flow meters, gas analysers, opacity monitors. 4) Keep records of fuel use, production, and emissions. 5) Submit reports on time. 6) Allow inspections.

Reporting: typically include total energy consumption, CO2 emissions, dust, SO2, and NOx. Use standard methods (e.g., IPCC guidelines for GHGs). Many regulators provide templates. If you donât have data, estimate using emission factors. But better to measure.

Compliance costs money but avoids bigger losses. For example, a smelter in Zambia was fined $50,000 for exceeding SO2 limits. Another in Egypt lost its licence for not reporting. Conversely, compliant smelters can access international markets â many buyers require environmental certification (ISO 14001).

Get help: industry associations (e.g., South African Institute of Foundrymen) offer training. Hire a consultant for initial compliance. Train a staff member as environmental officer. Keep a compliance calendar with deadlines. Budget for monitoring and reporting. Remember, regulations are tightening â what is voluntary today may be mandatory tomorrow. Stay ahead.

quiz.q: What is the typical electricity consumption for an electric arc furnace per tonne of steel?
quiz.explanation: Electric arc furnaces typically consume 400â600 kWh per tonne of steel.

quiz.q: Which energy source is commonly used in African smelters as a backup or for remote sites?
quiz.explanation: Diesel generators are commonly used for backup power or in remote locations.

quiz.q: What is a practical way to reduce electricity costs by shifting melting to off-peak hours?
quiz.explanation: Off-peak electricity rates are lower, so shifting melting can cut bills by 20â30%.

quiz.q: What percentage of fuel can be saved by preheating combustion air to 300Â°C using a recuperator?
quiz.explanation: Preheating combustion air to 300Â°C can save 15â20% of fuel.

quiz.q: What is a common heat recovery device for preheating combustion air?
quiz.explanation: A recuperator is a heat exchanger that preheats combustion air using waste heat.

quiz.q: What is the typical payback period for a heat recovery system?
quiz.explanation: Heat recovery systems often have a payback of 1â3 years due to fuel savings.

quiz.q: Which device is used to remove fine dust from off-gas?
quiz.explanation: Baghouse filters capture fine dust with high efficiency (up to 99%).

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a cyclone in off-gas treatment?
quiz.explanation: Cyclones are used to remove coarse particles from the gas stream.

quiz.q: Which chemical is commonly used to scrub SO2 from off-gas?
quiz.explanation: Both lime and caustic soda are used to scrub SO2 from off-gas.

quiz.q: How should collected hazardous dust be disposed of?
options: B) Stored in sealed bags and sent to licensed facility
quiz.explanation: Hazardous dust must be stored in sealed containers and disposed of at licensed facilities.

quiz.q: What is the approximate CO2 emission per tonne of steel produced?
quiz.explanation: Producing one tonne of steel emits about 1.8 tonnes of CO2.

quiz.q: What is the grid emission factor for South Africa (kg CO2 per kWh)?
quiz.explanation: South Africa's grid emission factor is approximately 0.95 kg CO2/kWh due to coal-heavy electricity.

quiz.q: Which fuel produces about 2.68 kg CO2 per litre when burned?
quiz.explanation: Diesel combustion emits about 2.68 kg CO2 per litre.

quiz.q: What is a way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in smelting?
quiz.explanation: Switching to cleaner fuels like natural gas or biomass reduces GHG emissions.

quiz.q: What is the carbon tax rate in South Africa as of 2024 (per tonne CO2e)?
quiz.explanation: South Africa's carbon tax is R120 per tonne CO2e as of 2024.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to find heat leaks in a smelter?
quiz.explanation: A thermal camera or infrared thermometer can identify hot spots and heat leaks.

quiz.q: What is the recommended oxygen level in flue gas for efficient combustion?
quiz.explanation: Target 2â3% oxygen in flue gas for efficient combustion; higher levels indicate excess air.

quiz.q: What device can save 30â50% of energy on fans and pumps?
quiz.explanation: VFDs adjust motor speed to match load, saving 30â50% energy on fans and pumps.

quiz.q: What is a no-cost energy efficiency measure?
quiz.explanation: Sealing furnace doors is a no-cost measure that reduces heat loss.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of preheating scrap using waste heat?
quiz.explanation: Preheating scrap reduces the energy needed in the furnace, lowering overall consumption.

quiz.q: Which regulation requires an Atmospheric Emission Licence in South Africa?
quiz.explanation: The National Environmental Management: Air Quality Act (NEMAQA) requires an Atmospheric Emission Licence.

quiz.q: Which Nigerian agency enforces air quality regulations?
quiz.explanation: NESREA (National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency) enforces air quality regulations in Nigeria.

quiz.q: What is typically included in an emission report to regulators?
quiz.explanation: Emission reports typically include energy consumption, CO2, dust, SO2, and other pollutants.

quiz.q: What is a consequence of non-compliance with environmental regulations?
quiz.explanation: Non-compliance can lead to fines, shutdown, and even imprisonment.

quiz.q: What certification can help access international markets?
quiz.explanation: ISO 14001 is an environmental management certification often required by international buyers.

quiz.q: What is a good first step to comply with regulations?
quiz.explanation: Identifying your regulator and understanding requirements is the first step to compliance.

quiz.q: What is the approximate CO2 emission factor for coke (kg CO2 per kg)?
quiz.explanation: Coke combustion emits about 3.1 kg CO2 per kg.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of measuring and reporting GHG emissions?
quiz.explanation: Measuring emissions helps identify energy savings and reduce costs.

quiz.q: What is a common heat recovery application for cooling water?
quiz.explanation: A plate heat exchanger can recover heat from cooling water for space heating or wash water.

quiz.q: What is the target for energy reduction in the module example?
quiz.explanation: The module suggests setting a target to reduce CO2 by 10% in two years.
